## Spatial Data Quality Toolkit

A small, focused suite for checking geospatial data before you trust
it. Free, no account, nothing ever leaves your browser. Want the full
explanation instead of just the tool? The
[interactive articles](/articles.html) walk through the same checks
in Python and R.

**[Inspect](geospatial-file-inspector.qmd)** →
**[Validate](geojson-shapefile-validator.qmd)** →
**[Check Topology](topology-checker.qmd)** →
**[CRS](crs-inspector.qmd)**

All four are live — Inspect, Validate geometry, Check Topology, and
find/convert a CRS.

## Raster Toolkit

Reading a GeoTIFF, then computing with it. **[Inspect](raster-inspector.qmd)**
→ **[Calculate](raster-calculator.qmd)** → **[NDVI](ndvi-calculator.qmd)**
→ **[Viewshed](viewshed-calculator.qmd)**: dimensions, bands,
resolution, CRS, NoData, and per-band value ranges first, then combine
two bands into a computed result — a difference map, a Normalized
Difference — shown as a colored overlay and downloadable as a GeoTIFF.
The NDVI tool specializes that same computation for vegetation
health, with red/near-infrared band presets. Viewshed answers a
different question — what's visible from a point, given the terrain
in between — and runs on R (Python is shown only as reference in its
[companion article](/posts/raster-viewshed.html), since no viewshed
implementation is available in this browser's Python runtime).

## GeoML Toolkit

Machine learning on spatial data, starting with unsupervised
clustering. **[Cluster](spatial-clustering-explorer.qmd)**: upload a
point file, set a distance radius and a minimum group size, and find
which points form dense groups — powered by DBSCAN, colored on the
map, downloadable. First tool in this family; more are planned.
